extracted.intended_audience: principal investigators and researchers preparing NIH grant applications (including new investigators) and grant administrators
extracted.subtask_short: allocating PI effort on NIH grants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and community experience about how much percent effort to request for a PI on NIH (and similar) grants, how effort interacts with budget review, institutional rules, and peer review judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of PI percent effort relative to project scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the percent effort listed for the PI matches the scope of work proposed and community/institutional norms (e.g., 25%, 40%, 50%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments note varying norms: 40% is 'totally normal' in some departments, 50% may be closely scrutinized, and >50% can draw attention. Reviewers may question whether a PI listing high effort is naive or not matching the stated roles. Consider aligning percent effort with the actual tasks you claim the PI will perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget appropriateness / reviewer scrutiny of budget
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the requested budget (including salary/effort) is appropriate for the project; reviewers are tasked with evaluating budget appropriateness even if budget is not part of the numeric score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget comments often appear on pink sheets or as guidance to council and may be elicited after voting. Reviewers may suggest reductions (e.g., reduce by ~100k). Non-modular (detailed/high) budgets can attract extra scrutiny from study sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total percent effort caps / cumulative effort across awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the PI's total committed effort across all grants (and institutional appointments) is plausible and does not exceed reasonable/allowed caps (e.g., avoid >90% total effort or impossible totals like >100% or 250%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators and commenters report advice not to go over ~90% total effort. Reviewers have rejected proposals that, combined with existing grants, implied excessively >100% effort. Be careful to account for existing commitments when proposing effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs involuntary cost sharing; salary cap implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether requested salary matches percent effort and whether the PI or institution is covering part of the salary (voluntary cost sharing) or being forced to (involuntary cost sharing due to NIH salary cap).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For PIs under the NIH salary cap, asking for less salary than %PE is 'voluntary cost sharing' and is permissible; for those over the cap institutions must involuntarily cost-share the excess. Ensure your institution permits voluntary cost sharing if you plan it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match between stated PI roles/tasks and percent effort (grantsmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the narrative roles and day-to-day responsibilities claimed for the PI align with the percent effort requested (e.g., listing daily data collection but also high-level responsibilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study sections may ding proposals if the PI's described activities don't align with the percent effort (e.g., PI still thinking like a postdoc and expecting to run all the data themself). This is presented as a grantsmanship issue: reviewers check if 'the PI knew what they were doing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: New investigator expectations and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Special considerations for new investigators (NIs) in setting percent effort; some allowance or different expectations may apply (e.g., higher effort often acceptable for NIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters report being comfortable with NIs listing high effort (even 100%) on first grants; program-specific rules (see BRAINS example) may require minimum effort. Be mindful of both study section culture and program RFAs for NIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-specific mandatory effort requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with explicit program or funder RFA requirements for minimum percent effort (e.g., BRAINS requiring at least 50%, exceptions for R00 requiring 75%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check RFA/institutional requirements: some awards mandate minimum effort and/or institutional letters attesting to percent research time (example: an agency requiring a letter that PI will devote 75% time to research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional support / hard-money vs soft-money context
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the PI's effort and salary requests reflect the level of institutional support (hard-money vs soft-money), with implications for reviewer perception and institutional letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 100% salary support on federal grants may suggest lack of institutional support. In hard-money environments (e.g., some Canadian grants) PI salaries are not requested and effort expectations differ. Make institutional support explicit when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of budget format (modular vs non-modular) and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: How the chosen budget format affects reviewer scrutiny: non-modular/bigger budgets draw more attention and can make the proposal a 'sitting target'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching to non-modular budgets (detailed, larger dollar amounts) can invite more budget comments and critique. Consider how the budget format will influence reviewers' focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of personnel effort (co-investigators, staff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the effort requested for co-investigators and other personnel is reasonable (e.g., co-investigator 10–15% may be questioned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers have dinged proposals for putting specific co-investigators on for too much effort. Amounts of other help requested are taken into consideration when evaluating PI effort and overall feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-PI / collaborative proposals: distributing effort across investigators
rubrics_metrics.description: How to allocate and justify percent effort when multiple PIs/collaborators are involved, especially when team members have different appointment types (soft vs hard money).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters highlight the challenge of dividing effort among 3–4 PIs, and that mixed appointment types complicate acceptable effort splits. Ensure clarity on each PI's role and whether the effort allocation reflects the workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of naivety or inability to manage project (PI competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may use effort allocation as a proxy for judging whether the PI understands the scope and can manage the project effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If effort allocation suggests the PI will personally do routine tasks that would typically be delegated, reviewers might conclude the applicant is naive. Demonstrate appropriate delegation and management commensurate with PI role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of salary/effort to project size and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether high salary or high percent effort for a single individual is justified given the overall project size and whether the work might warrant splitting into multiple grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 150K salary for one person on a modest R01 is questionable; a 700K/year R01 that effectively contains work for two grants may be seen as bloated. Justify why the proposed salary/effort is necessary and not artificially inflating costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and procedural notes about budget comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding that budget is not part of the numeric score but is reviewed and may lead to comments for council or later negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commenters note: 'budget shouldn’t affect score' (budget is not scored), though reviewers provide budget guidance post-vote. Expect budget critiques to be documented even if they don't change the initial priority score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to adjust effort after award
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical flexibility to change percent effort after funding (e.g., increase effort post-award if needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some applicants increased their effort after funding (one commenter increased to 75%). While you can often adjust effort post-award, plan initial effort and institutional approvals carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional policies restricting permitted percent effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Local institutional rules may cap permitted percent effort on grants (e.g., some institutions disallow 100% effort).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter noted their MRU does not permit 100% effort for anyone, for reasons including grant-writing obligations. Check institutional policies before committing to percent effort figures.
